title: Don't believe every word (I.4)
hookLine: a rumor lands in the family group chat; chapter four of the Imitation says weigh what you hear before you believe or pass it on
tomorrow: fancy old words or a plain Bible: which one tells the truth?

cards: A message lands in the family group chat. Somebody's cousin heard the parish is closing, the priest is leaving, and someone's in trouble. A shocked face.
A crying face. One person forwards it to another chat. Nobody asks where it came from.
A thumb hovers over the forward button. Chapter four of The Imitation of Christ was written for that thumb. Its first move is a single verb you can feel in your hands: weigh it.

teach.b: Don't believe every word or every impulse, the chapter says. A matter should be weighed carefully and patiently, before God. Then it names the reason, and it's honest about us.
People believe and speak evil of others more readily than good, it says, so weak are we. The wise don't easily credit every tale, because they know how human talk slides toward the worst version.
So the chapter gives a double piece of wisdom, and the second half is easy to skip.

teach.h: DON'T BELIEVE IT, DON'T PASS IT ON.
teach.b: Don't believe everything you hear. And don't rush to pass on what you've heard. Both.

Checking isn't enough if you forward it anyway. It leans on an older book of the Bible, the one the Douay-Rheims calls Ecclesiasticus, also known as Sirach, which says that someone quick to believe is light of heart.
And it closes with a practical move: take counsel from someone wise and conscientious, rather than following your own guess.

Here's the line to tell a friend tonight: a spiritual classic about following Christ stops, in chapter four, to talk about gossip. Because what we believe about each other shapes how we treat each other.

how: The Catechism counts rash judgment and detraction, believing or spreading harm about others without cause, as sins against the truth; Catholics bring these to confession and try to interpret others' words in the best light.

games.q: what does “don't believe every word” mean?
o: weigh what you hear before believing or repeating it
a rule against reading any text word for word
never trust anything that anybody tells you

p: evil of others, rather than good
don't rush to pass it on
quick to believe is light of heart

s: weighing what you hear means never believing anyone
it means patience and checking, and taking counsel from someone wise.
the chapter says people believe evil of others more readily than good
it names that weakness honestly, then asks for patience.
if you check a rumor yourself, it's fine to forward it while you check
the chapter has two halves: don't believe everything, and don't rush to pass it on.

games.q: your aunt shares a post claiming a saint predicted a disaster for next month. the family chat is buzzing. what does chapter four suggest?
o: weigh it: find the source before believing it or passing it on.
forward it; anything about a saint is safe enough to share.
reply that every story about a saint is made up anyway.
games.why: don't believe every word, the chapter says; weigh it patiently before God, and don't be quick to repeat what you've heard.

practice: Hold two things, one in each hand: a phone and a cup, a book and a set of keys. Don't guess from how they look; feel slowly which one is heavier, until you're sure.
That patience in your hands is the chapter's word for what you hear.

wordCard.voice: Don't believe every word. Chapter four's counsel: weigh what you hear patiently, and don't rush to repeat it.

orig.note: Latin, Imitation I.4: not every word is to be believed.

carryVoice: Your line: weigh it. Two hands and one pause, before anything gets forwarded anywhere. Sleep well.

sources.work: The Imitation of Christ (attributed to Thomas à Kempis)
